_note: Name-facts for China (FT-36, docs/PLAN_V0.8.md). See data/facts/italy.json
for the rules; the short version is one sentence, the first about the
NAME, and nothing the derived line already says.
China is the easiest country in the collection for this, because most of
its province names are literal descriptions of where the place is: a
side of a river, a side of a mountain, a side of a lake. Learn the half
dozen words and a third of the map reads itself - which is exactly the
kind of hook this second line is for.
bei / nan  = north / south      dong / xi = east / west
he = river (the Yellow)         hu = lake        shan = mountain
An id can be two places: a province and a city inside it sometimes
share one. Where the two are really the same place - Beijing, Tianjin,
Shanghai and Chongqing are municipalities - one list serves both. Where
they are not, as with Jilin the province and Jilin the river town, the
entry splits into region and city so a province fact is never shown
heilongjiang: "Black dragon river" — the Chinese name for the Amur, which is the border with Russia along the whole top of the province.
China's coldest corner: Harbin builds a city out of ice every winter, and −30 °C is an ordinary January morning.
Its border with Russia is 3,000 km long, and Heihe faces the Russian city of Blagoveshchensk across a river 600 m wide.
inner-mongol: Inner as opposed to Outer Mongolia, which became the independent country of Mongolia — "inner" meant nearer to Beijing.
A strip 2,400 km long wrapped across the whole top of China, bordering Mongolia and Russia.
It produces most of the world’s rare earths from one mine at Bayan Obo — the metals in every phone and wind turbine.

region: From Manchu girin ula, "along the river" — the Songhua, which the province's second city is built on.
Its eastern tip reaches within 15 km of the sea without touching it, cut off by a thin strip of Russia and North Korea.
Changbaishan on its Korean border is a volcano with a crater lake, and the source of three big rivers.
city: From Manchu girin ula, "along the river" — this city is the river town the whole province was named after.
Not the provincial capital, despite sharing its name: that is Changchun, 100 km west.
Its chemical works made it one of the first industrial cities of the People’s Republic, built with Soviet help in the 1950s.

xinjiang: "New frontier" — the name the Qing gave it in 1884, when it became a province rather than a conquest.
China's biggest region, a sixth of the country, and the farthest place on earth from any ocean.
Turpan sits 154 m below sea level and reaches 47 °C, watered by karez — underground channels dug from the mountains, some 2,000 years old.
liaoning: "Liao pacified" — ning is peace, and the Liao is the river running through it.
The old industrial heartland: coal, steel and the shipyards that built much of the navy.
Shenyang was the Manchu capital before Beijing, and its palace is the only other surviving imperial palace in China.
beijing: "Northern capital" — bei north, jing capital. Nanjing is the southern one, with the same second character.
It has been the capital, on and off, since Kublai Khan made it one in 1272.
The Forbidden City has 980 buildings and was closed to ordinary people for nearly 500 years.
tianjin: "The ford of heaven" — the crossing where an emperor forded the river on his way to take the throne in 1400.
Beijing's port, 120 km downstream, and the reason the capital could sit inland at all.
Nine countries held concessions here before 1945, so whole streets are British, French, German or Italian.
hebei: "North of the river" — he is the Yellow River, bei is north. Henan, on the same map, is the south bank.
It wraps almost entirely around Beijing and Tianjin, which were carved out of it.
The Great Wall meets the sea here at Shanhaiguan, the pass called the First Pass Under Heaven.
gansu: A portmanteau of two Silk Road garrison towns, Ganzhou and Suzhou — the same trick that names Jiangsu, Anhui and Fujian.
Its long thin shape is the Hexi Corridor, the only easy way between China proper and Central Asia, which is why the Great Wall ends out here at Jiayuguan.
The Mogao caves at Dunhuang hold 45,000 m² of murals painted over a thousand years by Silk Road travellers.
shanxi: "West of the mountains" — the Taihang range, which separates it from Hebei. Shandong is east of the same mountains.
Two thirds of China's coal has come out of here, and the plateau it sits on is made of wind-blown loess hundreds of metres deep.
Pingyao’s city walls and streets survive almost untouched from the Ming, because the town grew too poor to rebuild.
ningxia: "Pacified Xia" — the Western Xia kingdom the Mongols destroyed in 1227, remembered in the name of what replaced it.
The Yellow River irrigates a green ribbon through otherwise dry country; the rest is the edge of the Gobi.
It is the centre of Chinese wolfberry growing, and of the Hui, Chinese-speaking Muslims descended from Silk Road traders.
shandong: "East of the mountains" — the same Taihang range that names Shanxi, seen from the other side.
Confucius was born here, and Mount Tai has been climbed by emperors as a pilgrimage for two thousand years.
Qingdao was German from 1898 to 1914, which is why China’s best-known beer is brewed there to a Bavarian recipe.
shaanxi: Spelled with the double a on purpose: Shanxi and Shaanxi are the same syllables in Mandarin and differ only in tone, so the romanisation doubles a vowel to keep them apart on a page.
Xi'an, its capital, was the eastern end of the Silk Road and the seat of the emperor buried with the terracotta army.
The terracotta army was found by farmers digging a well in 1974, and about 8,000 figures have been counted.
qinghai: Named for the lake: Qinghai means "blue-green sea", China's largest, salt and 3,200 m up.
Both the Yellow River and the Yangtze rise here, within a few hundred kilometres of each other.
The Tibetan plateau here is the source of the water for nearly two billion people downstream.
henan: "South of the river" — the Yellow River again, the other bank from Hebei.
The floodplain where Chinese civilisation started, and the province with the most people after Guangdong and Shandong.
The Shaolin monastery is here, and Luoyang and Kaifeng were both imperial capitals long before Beijing.
jiangsu: A portmanteau, like several Chinese provinces: Jiangning (old Nanjing) plus Suzhou, the two cities that mattered.
Flat, wet and threaded with canals — the Grand Canal to Beijing runs the length of it.
Suzhou’s classical gardens, nine of them UNESCO sites, were built by retired officials as private landscapes in miniature.
anhui: Another portmanteau: Anqing plus Huizhou, two prefectures joined in 1667.
The Huangshan mountains here, all granite spires and pine trees in cloud, are the landscape Chinese painting keeps returning to.
Xuan paper and hui ink from here are what Chinese calligraphy has been written with for over a thousand years.
xizang: The Chinese name for Tibet: zang is the Tibetan region of Tsang, xi is west.
The highest region on earth, averaging over 4,500 m — and Everest sits on its border with Nepal.
The Potala Palace in Lhasa has 1,000 rooms and stands 3,700 m above sea level.
shanghai: "Upon the sea" — a fishing village's name that stuck to what became the largest city in the country.
Its older name, Hu, is still the single character on every local number plate.
The Bund’s waterfront banks were built by foreign powers between 1860 and 1940, and Pudong opposite was farmland until 1990.
hubei: "North of the lake" — Dongting Lake, with Hunan on the other side.
The Three Gorges Dam is here, the largest power station in the world by output.
Wuhan is where the 1911 revolution began that ended two thousand years of imperial rule.
chongqing: "Double celebration" — a prince marked two happy events at once in 1189 and renamed the city for them.
Not a province but a municipality, split from Sichuan in 1997 to manage the Three Gorges resettlement.
Built on hills so steep that a street can be the first floor of one building and the twentieth of another.
sichuan: "Four circuits" — four administrative districts of the Song, shortened; the folk reading "four rivers" is wrong but widespread.
A giant fertile basin ringed by mountains, and the home of the pandas — nearly all the wild ones live in its western hills.
The Dujiangyan irrigation system has watered its plain since 256 BC without a dam, and still works.
zhejiang: Named for the Zhe river, the old name of the Qiantang, whose tidal bore is the largest in the world.
Hangzhou was Marco Polo's "finest and noblest city in the world", and the Grand Canal's southern end.
Yiwu’s wholesale market has 75,000 stalls and supplies much of the world’s Christmas decorations.
hunan: "South of the lake" — Dongting Lake again, the mirror of Hubei to its north.
Mao was born here, and its cooking is the chilli-hot rival to Sichuan's.
Zhangjiajie’s sandstone pillars, hundreds of metres tall, were the model for the floating mountains in Avatar.
jiangxi: "West of the river" — an old Tang circuit west of the Yangtze.
Jingdezhen here has made porcelain for the imperial court for a thousand years, which is why fine china is called china.
Jingdezhen still fires porcelain in wood kilns, and the town has made almost nothing else for a millennium.
guizhou: "Precious region" — zhou is a prefecture, gui precious, a name given more in hope than description.
Karst country: limestone towers, caves and the biggest waterfall in China, and historically its poorest province.
The world’s largest radio telescope, FAST, sits in one of its limestone sinkholes, 500 m across.
fujian: A portmanteau of Fuzhou and Jianzhou, two prefectures of the Tang.
Mountainous and facing Taiwan across the strait; most overseas Chinese communities in South-East Asia came from here.
Its tulou are circular earth apartment houses, some holding 800 people, built for defence from the 1100s.
yunnan: "South of the clouds" — yun cloud, nan south: the land beyond the cloud-covered mountains, seen from the north.
China's wild elephants live here and nowhere else, in the tropical south on the Laos border, and the province has more plant species than the rest of the country combined.
It grows most of China’s tea and coffee, and the Three Parallel Rivers run through it in gorges only 70 km apart.
guangxi: "Broad west" — the western half of old Guang; Guangdong is the eastern half.
The limestone hills along the Li river at Guilin are the landscape on the back of the 20-yuan note.
Its Zhuang are China’s largest minority, 18 million people, with their own Tai-related language.
guangdong: "Broad east" — the eastern half of the same old Guang province.
Cantonese is its language, its cooking is what most of the world means by Chinese food, and it has more people than Germany.
Shenzhen was a fishing village of 30,000 in 1980 and is now a city of 17 million.
hainan: "South of the sea" — hai sea, nan south: the island beyond the strait.
China's tropical island province, on the same latitude as Hawaii, and its smallest by land.
Duty-free shopping has made it China’s holiday island, and it grows coconuts, mangoes and rubber.
harbin: Probably from Manchu, "a place for drying fishing nets", or from a Jurchen word for honour.
Russia built it in 1898 as a railway town, which is why it has onion domes and Russian streets.
Its ice festival carves buildings from blocks cut out of the Songhua river, lit from inside.
changchun: "Long spring" — an optimistic name for a city with bitter winters.
It was the capital of Japanese-run Manchukuo from 1932 to 1945, under the name Hsinking.
China’s first car factory and its first film studio were both built here in the 1950s.
urumqi: From a Mongolian or Dzungar word, "beautiful pasture".
It is the furthest city in the world from any sea, about 2,500 km in every direction.
The whole of China uses Beijing time, so here the sun can rise around 10 am in winter.
shenyang: "North of the Shen" — yang means the sunny, northern side of a river in Chinese geography.
It was the Manchu capital before Beijing, and its palace is the only other surviving imperial palace in China.
It was the centre of Chinese heavy industry and is the largest city in the north-east.
jinxi: "West of the brocade" — the name refers to Jinzhou, of which it was the western part.
It is now officially Huludao, "gourd island", for the shape of its peninsula.
It built and launched Chinese submarines and has a petrochemical industry.
baotou: From Mongolian baghatur, or from a phrase meaning "place with deer" — it is called the deer city.
The Bayan Obo mine here produces most of the world’s rare earths, the metals in every phone and wind turbine.
It is the largest city in Inner Mongolia and a major steel producer.
datong: "Great unity" — a name from a Confucian text describing an ideal society.
The Yungang grottoes here hold 51,000 Buddhist statues carved into cliffs from 460 AD, a UNESCO site.
The Hanging Monastery nearby is built on beams driven into a cliff face 75 m up.
tangshan: "Tang mountain" — named for the Tang dynasty emperor who camped there.
The 1976 earthquake here killed at least 242,000 people, one of the deadliest in recorded history.
China’s first railway and first modern coal mine were both built in this city in the 1880s.
dalian: Probably from a Russian rendering of a local name, or from a Chinese phrase about connected bays.
Russia built it as Dalny, then Japan held it as Dairen for forty years.
It is China’s northernmost ice-free port and its main gateway to Japan and Korea.
shijiazhuang: "The Shi family village" — it was exactly that, a village of about 500 people, until the railway arrived in 1902.
It is now the capital of Hebei with over ten million people in its prefecture.
Norman Bethune, the Canadian surgeon revered in China, is buried here.
taiyuan: "Great plain" — tai great, yuan a plain.
It has been a fortress city for 2,500 years and was the base from which the Tang dynasty seized power.
Its Jinci temple has halls from 1023 and is one of the oldest surviving wooden complexes in China.
yantai: "Smoke terrace" — beacon towers were built here in 1398 to signal pirate raids with smoke.
It is the largest fruit-growing area in China, particularly apples, and makes most of its wine.
Changyu, founded here in 1892, is the oldest winery in China.
zibo: A compound of Zichuan and Boshan, two towns joined in 1945.
It was the capital of the state of Qi, one of the most powerful of the Warring States.
The world’s oldest known football, cuju, was played here — FIFA recognises Zibo as the birthplace of the game.
jinan: "South of the Ji" — the Ji river, which no longer exists as a separate river.
It is called the city of springs: 72 named artesian springs rise inside it.
Its Baotu spring has been the subject of Chinese poetry for a thousand years.
qingdao: "Green island" — for an islet in its bay.
It was German from 1898 to 1914, which is why China’s best-known beer is brewed here to a Bavarian recipe.
Its old town of red-roofed German villas is unlike anywhere else in China.
lanzhou: "Orchid prefecture" — named for a nearby mountain.
It is the only Chinese provincial capital the Yellow River runs directly through.
Lanzhou beef noodles are a national dish, and the city was a staging post on the Silk Road.
linyi: Wang Xizhi, the calligrapher whose work is the model for all Chinese calligraphy, was born here.
Its wholesale markets are among the largest in northern China.
zaozhuang: "Jujube village" — the Chinese date tree that grew there.
Taierzhuang in it saw China’s first major victory over Japan in 1938.
The Grand Canal runs through the town, and a stretch of the old canal quarter has been rebuilt.
zhengzhou: "Zheng prefecture" — named for the ancient state of Zheng.
Shang dynasty walls from about 1600 BC survive in the city, among the oldest urban remains in China.
Its Foxconn plant assembles a large share of the world’s iPhones, and is called iPhone City.
xuzhou: One of the Nine Provinces of ancient Chinese geography, named in texts 2,500 years old.
It has been fought over constantly because four regions meet there; the 1948 Huaihai campaign decided the civil war.
Liu Bang, who founded the Han dynasty, came from this area.
xi-an: "Western peace" — renamed in 1369; it was Chang'an, "perpetual peace", for over a thousand years before.
It was the capital of thirteen dynasties and the eastern end of the Silk Road.
The terracotta army was found by farmers digging a well here in 1974, and its city walls are the best preserved in China.
suzhou: Its classical gardens, nine of them UNESCO sites, were built by retired officials as private landscapes in miniature.
The saying runs "above there is heaven, below there is Suzhou and Hangzhou", and it was the silk capital for a thousand years.
nanyang: "South of the mountain" — yang again meaning the sunny southern slope.
Zhang Heng, who invented the first seismometer in 132 AD, was born here.
Zhuge Liang, the strategist of the Three Kingdoms, farmed nearby before being recruited.
nanjing: "Southern capital" — the counterpart of Beijing, the northern capital.
It was the capital of six dynasties and of the Republic of China, and its Ming city wall is the longest ever built around a city.
The 1937 massacre here killed an estimated 200,000-300,000 people and remains a central issue between China and Japan.
hefei: "Confluence of the Fei" — two rivers of that name meet here.
It hosts China’s national laboratory for physical sciences and its experimental fusion reactor.
That reactor, EAST, has set world records for sustaining plasma.
nanchong: "Southern Chong" — named for its position relative to an older prefecture.
It is one of the oldest silk-producing areas in China, working the trade for over two thousand years.
Chen Shou, who wrote the Records of the Three Kingdoms, was born here.
chengdu: "Becoming a capital" — said to come from a phrase about a settlement becoming a city in three years.
The Dujiangyan irrigation system nearby has watered its plain since 256 BC without a dam and still works.
It is the home of the giant panda breeding programme and of Sichuan cooking.
wuhan: A compound of Wuchang, Hankou and Hanyang, three towns merged in 1927.
The 1911 revolution began here, ending two thousand years of imperial rule.
It sits where the Han meets the Yangtze and is called the thoroughfare of nine provinces.
hangzhou: Named as a prefecture in 589; hang may come from a legend about the emperor Yu mooring a boat.
It was the capital of the Southern Song and, in Marco Polo’s account, the finest city in the world.
Its West Lake is a UNESCO site and has shaped Chinese garden design for a thousand years.
ningbo: "Calm waves" — a name given in 1381 in hope of peace with Japanese pirates.
It has one of the busiest ports in the world by cargo tonnage.
Its Tianyi Pavilion, built in 1561, is the oldest private library in China.
nanchang: The 1927 uprising here is treated as the founding of the People’s Liberation Army, and 1 August is its anniversary.
Its Tengwang Pavilion has been rebuilt 29 times and is the subject of one of the most famous pieces of Chinese prose.
changsha: "Long sand" — for a sandbar in the Xiang river.
The Mawangdui tombs here held a woman buried in 163 BC whose body is the best preserved from the ancient world.
Mao attended school and became a communist in this city.
wenzhou: "Warm prefecture" — named for its mild climate.
Its merchants pioneered private enterprise in China from the late 1970s, a model called the Wenzhou style.
Wenzhou communities run businesses across Europe, particularly in Italy and France.
xiangtan: "Xiang pool" — a deep stretch of the Xiang river.
Mao Zedong was born in Shaoshan in this prefecture.
Qi Baishi, the painter whose work sells for more than almost any modern Chinese artist’s, was also from here.
guiyang: It is one of China’s main data centre hubs, chosen for its cool climate and cheap hydroelectricity.
Its Jiaxiu Pavilion has stood on a rock in the river since 1598.
fuzhou: It was one of the five treaty ports opened in 1842, and its shipyard built China’s first modern navy.
Most Chinese emigrants to New York come from this region, and its jasmine tea has protected status.
kunming: Named for the Kunming people, an ancient group recorded in Han dynasty texts.
Called the spring city for a climate that is mild all year at 1,890 m.
The Stone Forest nearby is a karst landscape of limestone pillars and a UNESCO site.
hechi: "River pool" — he river, chi a pool.
It has one of the highest proportions of centenarians in the world, particularly in Bama county.
It is largely Zhuang, China’s largest minority, and is mountainous karst country.
zhangzhou: Named as a prefecture in 686 for the Zhang river.
Its Yunxiao and Nanjing counties hold tulou, circular earth apartment houses built for defence, which are UNESCO-listed.
It is a major producer of narcissus bulbs and mushrooms.
xiamen: "Mansion gate" — from a phrase about the gateway to a great house, or a gate of the lower reaches.
Known to Europeans as Amoy, and the Hokkien spoken here spread across south-east Asia.
Gulangyu island off it, a former international settlement, is a UNESCO site with no cars and many pianos.
guangzhou: "Broad prefecture" — named in 226 AD; Europeans called it Canton.
Its Canton Fair has been China’s main trade exhibition since 1957.
Cantonese cooking and dim sum come from here, and it was the only port open to Western trade for much of the Qing period.
dongguan: "Eastern guan" — guan being a kind of grass used for weaving.
It became the workshop of the world in the 1990s, making a large share of global toys, shoes and electronics.
Humen in it is where Lin Zexu burned British opium in 1839, starting the First Opium War.
nanning: It is the capital of Guangxi and hosts the annual China-ASEAN Expo.
It is called the green city for its subtropical trees, and is about 160 km from Vietnam.
shenzhen: "Deep drains" — the name of a village, for the ditches in its paddy fields.
It was a fishing town of about 30,000 people in 1980, when it was made China’s first Special Economic Zone.
It is now a city of over 17 million and the headquarters of Huawei, Tencent and BYD.
haikou: "Sea mouth" — the mouth of the Nandu river.
The capital of Hainan and its main gateway.
Its Hai Rui tomb honours a Ming official whose dismissal for honesty became, four centuries later, the play that triggered the Cultural Revolution.
